findings.title: Queries are now interpolated twice in the shard-splitting path
findings.body: runShardSplitQuery() now calls datasource.applyTemplateVariables() on every target, and the resulting sub-requests are handed to runSplitQuery() (querySplitting.ts:296-299), which was changed in the same PR to also call applyTemplateVariables() on request.targets. Every shard sub-query therefore gets interpolated a second time (the new shard test even asserts applyTemplateVariables is called 5 times for a single target). Double interpolation re-runs variable/ad-hoc-filter/regex-escape logic over already substituted text: variable values that themselves contain `$`/`{{}}` syntax get expanded again, and ad-hoc filters (request.filters) can be appended twice to the selector, producing wrong queries. Interpolation should happen in exactly one place.

findings.title: Pre-interpolation can defeat the $__range split guard
findings.body: querySupportsSplitting() relies on isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr) to avoid splitting queries that use $__range (because the backend interpolates it per split range). Now that targets are interpolated before this check, any `$__range`/`$__range_ms`/`$__range_s` occurrence that templateSrv resolves on the frontend will already be substituted, so the guard no longer matches and the query gets split anyway — reintroducing the exact incorrect-range bug the guard was added for. The range check should run against the original, un-interpolated expression (or the guard moved before interpolation).

findings.title: Assertion on applyTemplateVariables call count encodes the double-interpolation behaviour
findings.body: The test now asserts `expect(datasource.applyTemplateVariables).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5)` for a single target. This number is an artifact of interpolation being re-applied inside runSplitQuery for each shard sub-request; it locks in the duplicate-interpolation behaviour and will break on any unrelated change to the number of shard groups, rather than testing that interpolation happens once up front.
